newsitem.title: CHINA: China steel chief says satisfied with bribery probe.
newsitem.headline: China steel chief says satisfied with bribery probe.

text.p: The chairman of big China steelmaker Capital Iron and Steel Corp said on Monday he was satisfied with results of a graft probe linked to his company, and that most missing funds had been recovered.
"I am satisfied with the investigation," said Bi Qun, who also is vice minister of metallurgical industry.
"Most of the funds have been accounted for," he told reporters after a news conference.

Bi did not give further details of the bribery probe of a former senior official of the Beijing-based steel manufacturing group -- a case that brushed senior levels of the Communist Party and one of the most politically powerful families in the country.
China's Supreme Court rejected an appeal in November of the suspended death sentence for Zhou Beifang, former chairman of Capital Iron and Steel's Hong Kong-listed affiliates.
Zhou is one of the so-called "princelings", or children of the communist elite who wield political influence because of their top level connections.
The Zhou family is close to the family of China's late paramount leader, Deng Xiaoping.

Zhou's father, Zhou Guanwu, was chairman and Communist Party chief of Capital Iron and Steel until he stepped down in February 1995, citing old age. He was 78 at the time and resigned only days after his son was detained.
Bi Qun was named to replace the elder Zhou.
Company officials and state media have never given a full account of the case.
The official media have said the younger Zhou accepted bribes between June 1993 and April 1994. It did not say who gave him the money or why.
He was also accused of paying bribes of 1.2 million yuan ($144,600 ) to two Beijing city officials to let his wife and daughter move to the British colony of Hong Kong.
Zhou's death sentence was suspended for two years. Such sentences are usually not carried out if the defendant cooperates with authorities.
Official media have said Zhou was treated leniently because he showed remorse and voluntarily returned ill-gotten funds.
